why: We use it for the one arrangement it states - the worship hall on one axis with the offering hall and the sanctuary - which is what puts the sanctuary behind the hall on the approach axis.

We use it for the fact that temple and shrine precincts were exempt land - the tax-free plot the campaign notes give the country monk. It defines the category and does not say how much such land an ordinary village temple held.

We use it for one thing - that at a Bishamon dedication the guardian pair at the entrance is tigers in place of the usual lion-dogs, which the page states outright. Its limits: one city temple in the shogunal capital, so it says nothing about a village shrine or about how common the form was; the one date it gives is 1848, at the very end of the Edo period, so the custom is attested late, not across the era; and the page itself calls the tiger pair "a rare sight" against the usual lion-dogs, which is why the rule it supports is the convention at a Bishamon dedication, not its reach.

We use it to corroborate the tiger pair as the general form at Bishamon temples, which it states as a rule rather than for one temple. Its limits: the sentence we rest on is a bare photo caption that cites nothing and names no temple, no period and no count, so it cannot date the custom or say how widespread it was; and it names a village Bishamon shrine in Iwate but describes nothing of its precinct.
We use it for the range of such grants, down to a single koku, which shows the small end existed. The smallest grants are not tied to village temples in the text.

We use it for the parish economy - the household entrusting its funerary rites to its temple and paying fuse - which is the "gifts and fees" of the campaign notes. It describes the system, not one temple's income.

We use it for who compiled the register - the village headmen, yearly - beside the temple's certification, which is why the country monk's records need a writing room and not a building. The quoted sentence is normative - what was to be done - rather than a description of observed practice.

We use it for the size of the ordinary earth-god shrine - a few square meters to over ten - to show that nobody lived in one; the form is old and the conclusion survives the discounts. Its limits: the shrines behind its size band are largely the rebuilds and factory-made concrete units of the post-1980 revival, a modern measurement of a premodern form; and its reach runs past the Chinese core into Taiwan and Southeast Asia.

We use it for a three-bay hall of 10 by 7 m, which stands at the large end of the earth-god shrines this record measures - a comparison this project makes against the few-square-meter shrines; the page itself never calls the temple large, and says its timber is smaller than comparable Yuan buildings. Its limits: one designated monument, a survivor selected for quality rather than a typical village shrine; a hall standing after three modern restorations; dimensions relayed from a gazetteer and a thesis.

unsettled: The 2.5 mu is a gazetteer figure for the temple as it originally stood, undated, so its period cannot be placed from the table.

why: We use it for where a Chinese village's population was registered - the lijia, not the temple. Its limits: resting on a single cited paper; and the lijia is a Ming institution that decayed under the Qing as fiscal reform and the baojia displaced it, so the registers were the state's under either name and never the temple's.

We use it for the statement that popular temples are run by local managers, village communities and lineages rather than by clergy - the standard characterization, corroborated in this record by the Mianning study's elected heads. Its limits: the quoted sentence sits in a section the encyclopedia flags as needing citations; and it is undated, describing the practice generally while our use projects it onto a premodern setting.
unsettled: The page is an undated general description of present practice that the record projects onto a premodern setting, so the table does not settle its period.

why: It gives the shape of Kaifeng's history under the Yellow River - the repeated floods that buried the city layer on layer - which is the extreme case a river-city map is measured against. Its limits are that the flood count we quote from it carries no citation on the page, so it is an uncited encyclopedia statement, with the peer-reviewed frequency in the peer-reviewed flood study cited beside it the better anchor; that Kaifeng under a perched, silt-choked river is the worst case of river-city danger and not the average; and that it is the Chinese half of a setting also modeled on Japan.

A paddy bund is a wall of piled mud whose height is set by how deep the water must stand, which has nothing to do with modern machinery, so the figure carries back to a premodern field. The honest limits are that the same chapter assumes modern fertilizer, pesticides and bred varieties; that it was written for tropical fish-farming projects in Africa and Southeast Asia rather than for a Chinese or Japanese paddy; and that a bund built to keep fish in is taller than one built only to keep water in, so we treat its 60 cm as the upper end of the range a paddy bund occupies rather than as a measured premodern height.

We use it for one thing only - that the village grove is a recognized, named class of woodland rather than a decoration we invented. It carries no count of groves per village and no grove area at all, so the sizes and numbers on our maps come from the survey papers and, where those run out, are marked as guesses.

It is the one large measured set of village grove areas the record could read - the annex over which our median, mean and spread of grove sizes are computed - and so it is what sizes the groves on our maps. Its limits are that the 115 woods were chosen as the most representative sites and the paper says the survey was not exhaustive, so our figures are statistics over a selected sample that plausibly drops the smallest and most degraded woods; that the paper scopes the feature to southern China, so its standing in for the wider East Asian practice is our assumption rather than its claim, made because no comparable Japanese survey could be read; and that the boundaries were drawn by judgment where a wood merged into secondary forest, so each area carries a convention.

The village grove is a feature we draw on nearly every map, and this gives the one thing hardest to guess - how big it actually is, and how much the sizes vary. The New Territories villages it surveys are Chinese villages, and their oldest wood predates British rule, so this is the Chinese custom our setting models, not a stand-in for it. It stands in only for Japan, whose village and homestead groves are a different custom that no public page we could read has measured; and the south China coast is subtropical, so the tree species differ from a northern or Japanese grove. The page says a wood is small because it is squeezed between the fields in front of the village and the hill behind, so these sizes are for villages backed by a hill; a village on open plain may have kept a grove of another size. The page rounds its figures and cites no study of its own, so where it disagrees with the underlying 2006 paper we follow the paper; and it gives the oldest wood's age of more than 300 years in a comparison table without saying how that age was established.

It is the only publicly readable survey we found that actually measures the planted grove at a village's mouth, and its numbers are what our maps size that belt of trees by - most groves under a hectare, and the village-entrance grove, the sugumagi that blocks the water mouth, averaging around seven tenths of a hectare and accounting for 42 of the 100 surveyed. Two limits stated plainly: it is Korean rather than Japanese or Chinese, cited because no comparable public survey of Japanese village groves could be read; and the groves measured are the ones that survive today, so a present-day area is only an approximation of the original planting.

It is the closest thing to a measured answer we could read on a public page to the question of how big a village's planted grove actually is and how many trees stand in it, so it sets the size band our groves are drawn to. Two honest limits: it is Korean, standing in for Japan and China because no comparable open survey of Japanese or Chinese village groves could be read; and it measures groves as they survive today, which records what has lasted rather than what was originally planted.

We use it for one concrete measure of a water-mouth grove - over a hundred mu (roughly seven hectares), nearly a thousand old trees, and fifty-six yews more than five centuries old - and the record treats that as the extreme end of the range rather than the ordinary case; a stand that has been kept at a village mouth for that long is evidence about the form even though the article around it is current news. Its limits: it is promotional about a government program; the numbers are the reporter's, unsourced; the article is in Chinese, and the passages the record quotes are this project's own translation; the grove is measured as it stands in 2022, not by any survey from the period: the village is a provincial "forest village" beside the Liugujian provincial nature reserve and its yews carry national protection, so the hundred mu is what survives under modern protection, not a record of the grove's premodern extent; the village sits at the Xin'an River's mountain source with its land 95% forested, where woodland cost a village far less than on a farmed plain; and the reporter calls it the largest, most varied and oldest water-mouth grove in East China, so nothing in it should be read as typical.

It carries the one number our ditches are drawn from - how tight a turn running water makes, measured against the channel's own width - together with the bank behavior that produces it. Its limits are that the radius it gives is the curvature a FREE channel settles into over years by cutting its own outer bank, while a farm ditch is dug and kept to a line, so its curve is set by whoever dug it and by the field boundary it runs along rather than by the water; and that it gives no figure for a maintained earthen ditch at all, so the step from a river's bend to a ditch's is this project's reasoning and not the article's.

We use it for one thing only, the legal confinement of the freight hand cart to Edo, Owari and Sunpu, which is what makes a cart the exception rather than the norm on a country lane, and for the article's note that freight carts were not permitted on the Tokaido until the Meiji period. Its limits are that it speaks for Japan alone, one half of this setting; and that it is about the regulated cities and highways, so it tells us what was forbidden outside them and nothing about what an ordinary village lane looked like.

It gives the one measured wheeled way we could read for premodern Japan, 2.7 m of route with a 90 cm center for the bulls, which sets the upper bound our village lanes are kept under: if a purpose-built cart road was nine feet across, an ordinary farm track was not wider. Its limits are that a paved road built to carry freight into the capital is the most exceptional kind of way there is and is not evidence of what an ordinary lane measured; and that it is Japanese, while China is this setting's leading reference.

It is what our whole picture of a Chinese country lane rests on - narrow paths wide enough for a walker and a barrow, cart tracks only on the eastern plains, and paths built for pedestrians, carrying-pole porters, barrow-pushers and litter-bearers - which decides the vehicle we draw a lane for. Its limits are that it is a readable route to Hommel and Needham rather than a primary source itself; that it is an advocacy publication whose standing thesis is that pre-industrial transport was more capable than it is remembered to be, so it reads its evidence in that direction; that it carries no width measurement at all - the paths it describes are 「scarcely wide enough for foot passengers and wheelbarrows」, which is a description and not a figure, so the width we draw a lane at is ours and not the article's; that its observations are early twentieth-century fieldwork used as a witness to a much older practice; and that its cart-track sentence speaks for the eastern plains, not for the rice-growing south our settlements are modeled on.

Every area a Japanese source states in tsubo, se or tan has to be turned into square meters before it can be drawn, and this is the conversion we use; the figures are exact definitions rather than measurements, so there is little for a source to be wrong about. Its limits are that the article's own values are the legally fixed modern definitions of units whose local sizes varied before they were standardized, so a premodern document's tsubo may not be exactly this tsubo; and - the one that can put a figure badly wrong rather than slightly - that the tan was redefined in the course of Hideyoshi's cadastral survey, from 360 bu to the 300 bu this page's tan assumes, so an area a pre-1590s document states in tan and we convert with this table comes out about a fifth too small. The tsubo itself is stable across that change, so an area given in tsubo is safe.

It is the plain definition of the structure our city maps draw and of what the watch on it was for, and it is the only source in the record that dates the institution and its spread, which is what settles whether a small unwalled seat would carry one. Its limits are that much of the article is about the surviving steel towers and the modern volunteer companies, so the premodern form has to be taken from its historical passages and not from what it shows standing today; and that its two datings do different work and must not be run together - it puts the ORIGIN of the tower in Edo-period Edo, the shogunal capital, but the SPREAD of the form across the country in the early Showa era, which is the twentieth century, so the fact that such towers became common everywhere cannot be used to put one in a small premodern settlement.

It supplies the one thing our fire-tower explanation needs beyond the tower itself: that the bell carried information by its cadence rather than simply making a noise, which is why a watchman on a tower is worth drawing, and it puts that bell on a tower within the period our settlements are pitched in rather than leaving it undated. Its limits are that its 1686 attestation is of the WORD in another of its senses, the bell of a striking clock, the earliest example it gives for the fire-alarm sense being dated 1706. Nor does it date the stroke code or say what size of place hung the bell: the encyclopedia entry among them describes the code in the same paragraph as the iron towers and pump sheds of the modern period, and ties the bell's spread to fire brigades it glosses with the Meiji-era term 消防組 (the national fire-brigade system of 1894), so it supports a bell on a tower in an Edo-period town but not in an Edo-period village, and its code cannot be dated to the Edo period from this page.

It tells us who actually manned, paid for and commanded an urban fire watch, which is the point our setting departs from deliberately, and it shows that the departure is narrower than it looks, since command sat with the magistrate historically as well. Its limits are that it is about Edo alone, the largest city in the country; and that it describes an institution of the long Tokugawa peace, so its scale and its politics do not transfer to a provincial city of the earlier, more martial period these maps are pitched in.

We use it for the transaction rather than the object: the amulet comes from the shrine or temple itself, and what the recipient gives back is understood as a donation to it, which is why our maps show no third-party stall selling charms at a temple gate. Its limits are that the word the article itself uses for the exchange is "sold", so "bestowed" is our own gloss on it and not the page's; that our conclusion goes one step further than anything the page states - it never says that nobody else sold charms at a gate, and we are reading that from its silence; and that the passages about factory manufacture and shop-sold versions describe MODERN commercialism, not the premodern practice our maps depict, so they cannot be read back into the setting.
unsettled: The page is undated and describes amulet practice as it is now, so the table does not settle whether the record takes a premodern or a present-day form from it.

why: It is our evidence that the approach to a great temple carries a settlement of its own, which is what puts shops, inns and lodging on a city map beside a temple rather than scattered anywhere. Its limits matter to how we read it: the article attributes the eating houses and souvenir shops a modern visitor pictures to the RAILWAY era, and names inns (hatago) as the premodern trade, so the crowded food-and-souvenir street is later than the period we draw.

It gives us what actually happens at a Chinese grave, which is what makes a burial ground a tended place on our maps rather than waste ground, and it names the paper goods whose makers we put among the funeral trades. Its limits are that it describes the festival as practiced rather than a historical period, so it cannot date anything; and that it says nothing about where the goods were made or sold, nor how far from a mound the tending reached, which is the figure our drawn collar would need.
unsettled: The page describes the festival as practiced and dates nothing, so the table does not settle whether its evidence is premodern or present-day.
The siting evidence is an undated photograph of a surviving walled village, so the table does not settle its period.

why: It is our evidence that a hall of this kind fronts a hard open plaza where the lineage gathers and holds its ceremonies, which is why our maps keep swept open ground before a religious building instead of packing houses to its door. Its limits are that it describes the Cantonese ancestral HALL of one southern county, not the earth-god shrine we pair it with and not northern practice; that it is written about halls that are still standing, and where it does sort them by period it is dating the BUILDINGS, while every sentence it gives about the plaza carries no period at all - so it says what such a forecourt is for and nothing about when the arrangement began or how old the one we draw would be; and that it says nothing about grain-drying, markets or opera on that ground.
unsettled: Every sentence about the plaza carries no period, and the halls are dated only as buildings, so the table does not settle the period of the arrangement.

why: It is the practice that lets our maps put a settlement's burial ground at the edge of the fields while the stone that a family visits stands at the district's temple - two places for one dead person, which is otherwise hard to credit. Its limits are stated on the page and we keep them: the custom is concentrated in the Kinki region and merely scattered elsewhere, so it is a regional form rather than a national norm.

It is why the ground around a shrine is drawn swept but the trees around it are drawn standing: the grove is deliberately KEPT, the opposite of cleared, so our sweeping rule touches only the loose scatter and never the wood. Its limits are that it is a tertiary summary with no measurements - no depth, no species count, no distance from the hall - so it gives the principle and none of the numbers.

It is our readable witness that ordinary hamlets buried their own dead at their own fringe, which is what sets a burial ground at the edge of a settlement on our maps, and it describes the cremation site as a dug pit with no building, which is what keeps our drawn cremation ground bare. Its limits are considerable and worth naming: it is one person's compilation with photographs rather than a survey; it gives no areas or distances at all; the grounds it photographs are twentieth-century survivals rather than sites dated to any premodern century, so they witness a custom that lasted into living memory rather than one we can date; and it speaks for one prefecture.

We use it for one fact: the village graveyard held in common by its own inhabitants is a recognized kind of place, which is what justifies drawing one ground for a settlement rather than scattered family plots. Its limits are that it gives no size, no siting rule and no period for the village form, and that it gives no household threshold and nothing on the disused grounds left standing.
unsettled: The page is largely about present-day regulation and gives no period for the village form, so the table does not settle which period the record takes from it.

why: It describes the bridge our maps draw, and it states the mechanism that sets an abutment back from the water: a shallow strip footing cannot be sunk below the depth the current will scour, so the bank is armored instead and the footing kept clear of it. Its limits are that the only distance in it is an illustrative worked example rather than a rule, and is measured from the crest of the bank slope rather than from the water; and that it is American, standing in for a practice no premodern East Asian source we could read describes.

It is the direct evidence for the countryside our lanes are drawn for - no horse-drawn carriage at all before Meiji, inhabitants on foot or on horseback, goods on a horse's back. It is also precise where the general account is loose: the highway cart prohibition was to keep the post-horse system supplied with horses, not to spare the road surface, and the causes it names include the kind of horse rather than the size of one. Its limits are that it is a short conference paper rather than a monograph; and that it gives no road widths and no lane dimensions of any kind.

It gives the width of the trunk highways in ken, and it is careful in exactly the way that mattered to us: it states the ordinary figure with mountain roads expressly excluded, so the two are not to be confused. Its limits are that it cites no survey behind the number; that it gives no figure at all for the mountain roads it excludes, so that narrowing remains unsourced; and that a second readable account of the same highways gives a wider ordinary width, so the two bracket the figure rather than confirm it.

It is the second readable account of a trunk highway's width, and it disagrees with the first - 4 ken as the ordinary width, rising to 7 or 8 ken in places - which is why our record brackets the figure instead of stating one. Its limits are that the explanation it offers for the width is a military one, which suits the greatest highways and not an ordinary road; and that it says nothing about mountain roads or about the barriers.

It carries the fact our lanes depend on - that bulk goods in Ming China moved by water, in quantities no road could have taken - with the 1472 decree of four million shi a year to the canal terminal outside Beijing and the abandonment of the sea route. Its limits are that it describes the state's own grain traffic rather than ordinary trade; and that it does not characterize the feeder canals as a dense net; and that it says nothing about Japan, whose water freight stays uncited.

It states as a principle the thing our shop-house bands are built on, work and dwelling in one building, and it says which part of the plan is shop and which is home, so a merchant family living behind its own storefront is no longer general reading. Its limits are that the Kyo-machiya is the most developed and most urban form of the type, so an ordinary county-seat shop would be plainer, smaller and less deep; and that it gives no dimensions a map could use.

It is the closest attested analogue to the caravan inn our town maps draw, and the only account read that describes the whole arrangement rather than just naming the institution; it is also what contradicts the drawn inn's second story, since it says the buildings in the yard were uniformly single-story. Its limits are that it describes a twentieth-century survival in Manchuria rather than a Ming or Edo inn, and in the north rather than in the rice-growing south this setting also leans on; and that it counts nothing - no animals, no rooms, no dimensions - so every size on our sheet remains ours.

It settles that a highway inn of two stories is a real Japanese building and not an invention of this project's drawing. Its limits are the reason it does not settle the drawing. Nothing read describes a cart yard, a long stable, a feeding trough or a grooms' lean-to at a lodging house of this kind - this article describes the building and its rooms and says nothing of a yard at all - so it is no evidence for the fittings the wagon inn our maps draw is built around, and an analogue for a different institution. It is one building, and an exceptional one selected by its own survival: 大旅籠 names it the great hatago of its town, and its proprietors ran a pawnshop beside the inn and served as post-station officers, so it is the leading house of the street rather than the ordinary one on it. Its date, about 1836, is the very end of the period this setting draws on, and the station system it belongs to is that institution in its mature nineteenth-century form. The registration record it summarizes was not read. Nothing read says inns of its kind were usually two stories. And its ground-floor room list mixes the building's historical rooms with its present museum fabric - an exhibition room stands in the same list as the parlor and the kitchen, and the upper floor the citation rests on holds mannequins of two literary travelers at dinner.

It gives the fallback orientation of our magistrate's manor as a rule rather than a preference - the seat sits to the north and faces south, by the regulation for a local government office and by ritual propriety - and the terms behind it mean proper rather than lucky, so the orientation is the formal one and not an auspicious one. Its limits are that it describes one surviving building of one dynasty; and that it is Chinese office regulation standing in for a setting drawn from pre-Meiji Japan as well as from imperial China.

It states where a government's offices stand - inside the castle, with the ruling house's own mansion, at the apex of a hierarchy the whole samurai quarter is arranged around - which is our rule that offices cluster on the grandest compound rather than floating mid-block. Its limits are that it describes one very large castle town of one of the greatest domains, so a county seat's handful of offices is a much smaller thing; and that it works in quarters and hierarchies rather than dimensions, so it sizes nothing on our sheet.

It is the evidence that the number of wells in a farming community was a governed quantity fixed by the residents themselves - a permit bought with a fee, a survey of the wells standing, a cap negotiated between the upper and the lower villages, and patrolmen the villages provided for each other - with the local government expressly declining to interfere inside the levee. (The permit fee is this paper's; the sibling entry on the same institution records that the 1812 agreement carries no such charge and that the only money runs the other way, so the two accounts differ and the record should not lean on the fee.) It also corrects the reason: the quarrel was not scarcity but its opposite, the drainage the upper villages' artesian wells poured onto the lower villages' paddy. Its limits begin with the era: the institution the paper documents was established around the 1850s and ran to about 1905, so most of its recorded life is Meiji rather than Edo, and it reaches the setting's period only at the very end. Beyond that: it is one institution on one ring levee; that the cap is a total across the whole levee allotted among villages rather than a rule per village in the abstract; and that it is a working paper in a repository rather than a journal article, though a companion study of the same institution by the same scholar is registered here separately.

We use one sentence of it: northern China's 400 to 800 mm of annual rain, concentrated in summer showers, which is the rainfall that leaves a dry field there chronically drought-exposed and makes a well worth sinking in the middle of one. Its limits are that its region is defined by isotherms and isohyets and takes in both the north-China plain and the loess provinces, so it fits our sentence's own conflation of the two better than it fits either strictly; and that everything else in the paper - the drought indices, the satellite productivity data, the trends - is about the present day and is used for nothing here. The sentence we do take is the paper's own uncited description of where it worked, not a result it measured.

It names the five fixed grades of the Chinese irrigation ladder in order - main, branch and lateral as the canal system proper, farm and field as the in-field distribution - and puts the maoqu at the bottom of it, laid out to the size of the individual basin and, usefully for a map of a hamlet, dug by the farmers themselves. That is what tells us where the drawn net honestly stops and what lies below the last channel we can draw. Its limits: a municipal standard of 2010 for consolidated, machine-worked land, and it gives no dimensions we use; and its PDF's embedded font inserts spaces between characters and a filler glyph at some clause starts, so a machine reading it and a person reading it see different strings.<!-- our quotation reproduces the text layer as it renders and gives the clean form beside it -->

unsettled: The survey of 1975-76 records practice remembered as customary, which falls after Japan's cut-off of about 1955 yet describes hand transplanting, so the table does not settle its period.

why: It measures the gap between two ranked gates and the way between them: from the first torii to the second at the precinct entrance is about 300 meters, and the approach is a little over 7 meters (4 ken) wide, on an approach whose horseback archery the page dates to the Kamakura period. Its limits are that one shrine is one instance rather than a distribution; and that what the page dates to the Kamakura period is the PRACTICE and the place name - the 300 m and the 7 m describe the approach as it now stands, and nothing on the page says either is unchanged.

It states where a village's tutelary hall stands: usually built at the village's water mouth, the shuikou, with a named surviving instance built in 1760 on the bank of a stream in what is now Sanzhi, New Taipei. That is the geometry our village shrine follows, dated and on a watercourse rather than asserted in the abstract. Its limits are that its "usually built at the water mouth" is the encyclopedia asserting a custom rather than a survey of where such halls stand, so the record holds one dated instance and a generalization; that the deity so sited is a Hakka tutelary of Tingzhou and Zhangzhou origin rather than the earth god this record's own prose names; and that its instances are Taiwanese Hakka settlements, one regional tradition rather than a general Chinese rule.

It gives the mound's base beside its height - about 49 m (30 ken) across, 7.2 m (4 ken) high, under a five-ring stone pagoda about 9 m tall - and that base is the anchor for how wide a monumental bone mound is drawn, which nothing else read supplies. Its limits are that it names no source for its figures; that the mound is a monumental war memorial rather than an ordinary funerary feature, so it bounds the top of the range and not the middle of it; that the figures are of the mound as it now stands, after later repair and its stone fence; and that the national historic-site designation file, which would carry surveyed dimensions, could not be opened.

It states the rule our wayside shrines are placed by, and states it as an organizing idea rather than a list: the deity is enshrined at spatial and social boundaries - a village's entrance and exit, a mountain pass, a crossroads, the foot of a bridge - standing by the roadside as a stone monument or image to ward off epidemics and evil spirits coming from outside. That is the landing, the crossing and the gate our city shrines mark. Its limits are that it is a tertiary encyclopedia which carries a sourcing-deficiency notice over the very sections the placement sentence sits in; that it does not put such a shrine at a wellhead, which this record had also claimed. It is a different work from the walking-tour company's English page on the same deity, which the record also cites.

Three independent reference works agree on the form our gate quarters take: a settlement built in a street-village shape along both sides of the pilgrimage road, where merchants and craftsmen raised shops for the worshippers, with inns and shops and craftsmen's shops gathering, and lodging and commerce as the principal livelihood - the frontage following the approach, which is the map-relevant part. The Britannica entry adds the eating-and-drinking establishments as what was added to the festival market once it became permanent. Its limits are that none of them puts a sweet-seller at the gate, which is why that trade is cited to the highway teahouses instead.
